title: Bar Charts and Histograms 📊
description: Create vertical and horizontal bar charts, stacked bars, and histograms to show distributions.

slides.title: Bar Charts: Comparing Categories 🆚
slides.content:
# When to Use Bars

Bar charts are perfect for:
- Comparing values across categories (e.g., sales by product)
- Showing rankings
- Visualizing counts

Pandas offers `kind='bar'` (vertical) and `kind='barh'` (horizontal).

slides.title: Category Data
slides.content: Create a simple DataFrame for bars:

slides.title: Vertical Bar Chart 📊
slides.content:
## `kind='bar'`

```python
sales_by_product.plot(kind='bar', title='Sales by Product')
```

The index becomes x‑axis categories, column values become bar heights.

slides.title: Bar Chart Example
slides.codeSnippet: sales_by_product.plot(kind='bar', color='skyblue', edgecolor='black', title='Sales by Product')

quizData.question: What determines the height of each bar in `df.plot(kind='bar')`?
quizData.explanation: Each numeric column's value determines the bar height for that category.

slides.title: Horizontal Bar Chart ↔️
slides.content:
## `kind='barh'`

Swaps x and y axes. Good when category names are long.

```python
sales_by_product.plot(kind='barh', color='coral')
```

slides.title: Grouped and Stacked Bars 🧱
slides.content:
## Multiple Columns

If you have more than one column, bars are grouped side‑by‑side by default. Use `stacked=True` to stack them.

```python
df.plot(kind='bar', stacked=True)
```

This is great for part‑to‑whole relationships.

slides.title: Stacked Bar Chart
slides.content: Let's create a DataFrame with two products:
slides.codeSnippet:
df_multi = pd.DataFrame({
    'Product': ['A','B','C'],
    'Q1': [100,150,120],
    'Q2': [130,140,160]
}).set_index('Product')
print(df_multi)
df_multi.plot(kind='bar', stacked=True, title='Quarterly Sales by Product')

quizData.question: What does `stacked=True` do in a bar chart?

options.text: Stacks the values on top of each other for each category

quizData.explanation: Stacked bars show cumulative totals per category.

slides.title: Histograms: Distribution of a Single Variable 📊
slides.content:
## `kind='hist'` or `df.hist()`

A histogram groups numeric data into bins and shows frequency. Use it to understand the distribution of a column.

```python
df['column'].plot(kind='hist', bins=20)
```

Alternatively, `df.hist(column='col')`.

slides.title: Histogram Example
slides.content: Generate random data and plot histogram:
slides.codeSnippet:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)
heights = pd.Series(np.random.normal(170, 10, 1000))
heights.plot(kind='hist', bins=30, color='purple', alpha=0.7, title='Distribution of Heights')

quizData.question: What does the `bins` parameter control in a histogram?

options.text: The number of intervals (buckets) the data is split into

quizData.explanation: More bins give finer granularity; fewer bins give a smoother overview.

slides.title: Density Plot Overlay 📈
slides.content:
## `density=True`

To show probability density instead of frequency, set `density=True` (or `normed=True` in older versions). Often combined with a `kind='density'` plot.

```python
heights.plot(kind='density')
```

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Multiple Histograms in One Chart

Plot two columns as histograms by calling `df[['A','B']].plot(kind='hist', alpha=0.5)` to overlay semi‑transparent histograms.
